#3290. ‘Hejira’ at 50: Beck, Cameron Crowe, Clairo, and More Honor Joni Mitchell’s 1976 Masterpiece

J oni Mitchell wanted to go ice skating. It was February 1976, and she was standing on the edge of a frozen Lake Mendota in Madison, Wisconsin, wearing a black ermine cape and a black wool hat. All she needed were black skates to match. “I had a hell of a time getting the guy to give me black skates,” she recalled to Cameron Crowe, decades later. “He said, ‘Black skates are for, for men, madam.’ I said, ’No, no, you don’t understand. I’m having a funeral for my dead tour. I need black.”

Mitchell had recently cancelled the remainder of her Hissing of Summer Lawns tour, performing her last show at the nearby Dane County Memorial Coliseum. She was exhausted, battling a cocaine addiction, and reeling from the breakup with her drummer John Guerin, which she’d later describe as “one of the most special relationships” she’d ever had. This was her wake for it all, a farewell ride through the ice — not so different from the “River” she dreamt about skating on just five years prior. The ice was starting to thaw, and there were loud crashing sounds coming from the nearby trees, a sound she likened to “cases of Coca-Cola smashing.” She began to skate anyway, her black outfit standing in stark contrast to the backdrop.

Legendary photographer Joel Bernstein captured this moment, which would eventually appear inside the gatefold for her next album: Hejira. On the front cover, taken by Norman Seef, she’s wearing a black beret and holding a cigarette, stoically staring at the camera (she wanted it to look like an Ingmar Bergman film, she said), as a wide, open road is juxtaposed below. The artwork indicated the mission statement of Hejira — in the same way she skated away on that ice and didn’t look back, Mitchell got in her car and drove. “The Hejira album was written mostly while I was traveling in the car,” she told Crowe, in her 1979 Rolling Stone cover story. “That’s why there were no piano songs, if you remember. Hejira was an obscure word, but it said exactly what I wanted. Running away, honorably.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Mitchell took three journeys while making Hejira: a portion of Bob Dylan’s all-star Rolling Thunder Revue Tour in late 1975, her short-lived Hissing trek in early 1976, and a cross-country drive she made in a white Mercedes without a license (she’d often wear a red wig in disguise, and go by names like Charlene Latimer and Joan Black). Released in November 1976, the album is a timeless travelogue of jazz-folk magic, when Mitchell left it all behind in search for more. “I’m porous with travel fever,” she sings on the aching title track. “But you know I’m so glad to be on my own.”

It’s impossible to pinpoint the genius of Hejira on just one track. There’s the opener “Coyote,” about the affair she had with the playwright Sam Shephard on the Rolling Thunder tour. That song is now immortalized in a viral video from Martin Scorsese’s documentary, where she casually performs it for a stunned Dylan, Roger McGuinn, and Gordon Lightfoot. There’s “Furry Sings the Blues,” about her encounter with the Memphis blues legend who didn’t exactly take a liking to her (yes, that’s her longtime pal Neil Young on the harmonica). The stunning “Amelia,” named after Amelia Earhart, was her ode “from one solo pilot to another …sort of reflecting on the cost of being a woman and having something you must do.” Hejira is arguably her most cohesive body of work, featuring the fretless bass of Jaco Pastorius — whom she called the bass player of her dreams — plus guitarist Larry Carlton, percussionist Bobbye Hall, and others.

Looking back, Mitchell knew she was at the height of her powers. “I feel a lot of people could have written ’Chelsea Morning,’” she said. “But I don’t think anyone else could have written the songs on Hejira.” In honor of the 50th anniversary of Hejira, Rolling Stone spoke with musicians and actors about its legacy, and why it continues to resonate with listeners today. And in a full-circle moment, Crowe, who is currently working on a Mitchell biopic, pays tribute to the record he discussed with Mitchell in this very magazine, all those years ago. Related Content Clairo Covers Beloved MF Doom Song With El Michels Affair 'Grief Is Universal — And Very Specific': Diana Silvers on Her Devastatingly Beautiful New Record See Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis Spoof 'You Can See Everything' Beck Regrets Turning Down ‘Zoolander’ Character That Went to David Bowie

I’ve been a Joni Mitchell fan for a really long time, since I was a kid. And one of my best friends who passed away, we were obsessed with her. She was the one who actually introduced me to Joni Mitchell through Blue, because we would just listen to the album all the time. So through a general obsession with her, I just eventually went through all of her albums. And I really remember being particularly attached to Hejira when I was a teenager. I would go on long walks around my neighborhood [in Oak Park in Illinois], listening to that album, and just be really emotional.

Jaco’s bass literally captures the feeling of being on a trip and moving. He uses his bass as a vehicle on that album in such a cool way. And Joni’s lyrics feel like being on a road trip, listening to somebody’s stories. It reminds me of being with my parents, driving. We always drive from Chicago to Georgia where my family’s from, and just being on the road and talking.

The album itself feels like a departure. She’s going on a journey and choosing to go away from the industry for a minute, and that is captured sonically in a really interesting way. With Hejira, she distills the feeling of loneliness in a way that she hadn’t done before. Each song is dealing with loneliness, but she puts it into these different scenarios and narratives. They all come together to tell this one story of being a woman who’s alone, just traveling.

In Martin Scorsese’s film The Rolling Thunder Review: A Bob Dylan Story, there is a moment where Joni plays her new song, “Coyote,” at Gordon Lightfoot’s house. I love that there is footage of the early creation of this song. The lyrics change a little on the album, but you can see in her eyes the memories are very powerful as she sings and remembers. She had just written “Coyote” on a bus when she was with the tour, as she looked out at the “white lines on the freeway,” after she had a brief, tumultuous affair with the playwright Sam Shepard. Most of us have had these youthful, quick assignations, and I love being in her head as she reconciles the moment through her poetry and lyricism. Hejira is filled with emotion and hunger and as a young woman. Hejira helped me with the complexities of life, love, and longing.

It’s something that stayed with me my whole life. Being somebody who makes records and always having trouble listening to records because you’re just always thinking about technically how they were made, it’s a beautiful example of just being so disconnected from any kind of process. It doesn’t bear examination. I just find it 100 percent an emotional reactive experience. It conjures up something that I am so desperate to hold onto in my life. Basically what I’m saying is, I’m just a sad, pathetic fan, really.

Those things get chipped away gradually, as you meet all your heroes and make a lot of music. You never really listen to music the same way. But I’m a teenager again when I listen to it. I don’t know if it’s the imagery or the fact that she has this incredible way of weaving a narrative that is just so difficult to do in song. I mean, poetry is powerful, but the combination of melody and poetry is this kind of witchcraft that has always cast a spell on me.

She’s my favorite artist. And this record is an apex of confidence. She’s really just doing what she wants, to the nth degree. She’s this crazy sort of enigmatic, weird figure. You hear all these stories about her. She’s a manifestation of something that is so rare and special that my version of her that I have in my heart and my idea of who she is, I’m just clinging onto it for dear life. It’s like a hero I never want to meet. She could be the nicest, warmest person on Earth, but she wouldn’t be this person that she’s created in my mind personally, by my personal relationship with her music.

I remember hearing a long time ago that Joni wrote most of Hejira while she was on a road trip across America, and ever since then, I’ve always listened to it on long drives. It just makes so much sense to me. The whole record feels like it’s constantly moving, whether you’re speeding down a highway or sitting in traffic watching the sun go down.

As a drummer first, I’m always listening for the drums and percussion on records. To me, they’re kind of the heartbeat of any modern album. I know a lot of Joni’s records don’t have much drumming on them, but the fact that Hejira is constantly chugging along without a lot of full kit drumming continues to blow my mind. And I think Jaco’s bass playing adds this whole other rhythmic dimension to her music.

I’ve always thought of Joni as a percussionist in her own way. The way she attacks the guitar strings, the rhythms she creates with her strumming, it’s unlike anything I’ve ever heard from another musician. It’s one of the most fascinating things about her playing to me. And then you have Jaco on bass, another absolute master of rhythm, and the two of them create this incredible, almost hypnotic pulse that runs through the whole record.

And Bobbye Hall’s percussion adds so much to that feeling. It’s never overpowering, but there’s so much movement and texture in what she’s doing. All these little rhythmic details that somehow make the music feel even more alive. Between the three of them, there’s this constant sense of motion, like the music is always pushing forward but never in a hurry to get anywhere.

Hejira was the Joni album that helped me meet Joni. I feel like her truest self comes through on this record so beautifully, and it’s an anchor on tour when the roads are never ending and the bus forever rumbling. My favorite song is “Coyote.”

Hejira is Joni’s culmination to my mind. Her greatest songs, the greatest band, the greatest recordings, the most revelatory. The signature Roland Jazz Chorus guitar amp tone. Jaco Pastorius truly unleashed. The concepts and material mined into their seventh and eighth minute in some cases. I like to believe her whole catalog was leading to this moment. She’s at the height of her powers, and the masterworks that follow (Don Juan’s Reckless Daughter, Mingus, Night Ride Home, Turbulent Indigo, etc.) feel possible because of what Hejira unlocked. The writing is perhaps the most challenging, but the experience remains incredibly propulsive; you’re carried along by bearing witness to a human truly unrestrained by self-doubt, by adhering to any kind of rules or any kind of culture, someone in the midst of their quest to express their purest self. Maybe that sounds vague, but anyone that knows the record knows exactly what I’m talking about. When I’ve been asked about it, I’ve jokingly replied, “It’s as far as music has come.” But maybe that’s actually true.

I was touring extensively through my twenties, and I think it was at least 10 months of the year I was just on the road constantly. It was such a grind, but music had become a companion. We all had our headphones, and you’d sit on these long plane rides and bus rides listening to records. So it’s a lot of time to take a lot of deep dives. The whole Odelay tour, I was listening to Joni on the bus. It was pretty much Joni, Françoise Hardy records from the mid Sixties, and Morricone soundtracks — but not the Westerns, the weirder stuff. And then I had a CD of a rainstorm in Hawaii. That was all I listened to. It was like Joni and a Hawaiian rainstorm.

Hejira is the sound of an artist who has evolved so deeply into their own voice and their own craft. It’s a thing to behold. It’s a place that not a lot of artists even get to. Either they’re not really on that search to cultivate that rarefied place in their work, or they’re distracted by success and fame and touring, which happens to anybody who gets caught up in the sort of mechanics of the music business. So I think it’s even more of a singular achievement that she was able to make this after being on such a nonstop, relentless decade of making albums and touring. Usually at that point, somebody would just want to disappear for five years.

The music doesn’t necessarily sound like anything she had done before. One thing that’s really striking to me is the guitar sound. The effect on her guitar is a chorus pedal. The first one came out the year she was making the record. This was brand new technology. So this is like, “This new weird thing came out, and I’m going to put it on my entire album.” Not even, “Let’s vet this and see if this is cool. Is this going to be trendy? Is this going to sound dated?” This chorus pedal becomes the sound of whole genres afterwards. I don’t think it really becomes part of the palette of popular music till maybe the early 2010s. You listen to almost all of indie rock, from Mac DeMarco, to pop artists.

And then you also get the guitar sound of Prince’s Purple Rain, which comes from this record, without a doubt. It is interesting that something that is uncompromising, and not even her most popular album or most iconic, still managed to have an imprint on pop. Honestly, I think the sound of this even filters into shoegaze and Cocteau Twins. I don’t know if people have put those things together, but I see it clearly.

She is so mature as an artist on this record. I mean, it would take you more than a lifetime to get to that maturity. Somehow, she did it.

I first listened to Hejira in full on a tour bus driving through Europe. Highway rushing past, barren fields and long stretches of countryside out the window, the way Joni intended (I think). It struck me immediately as a timeless record. None of the songs are shorter than four minutes, the longest one being almost nine, but somehow they all feel intentional. She doesn’t waste words. I was so intrigued by that concept, of letting the story speak for itself, and setting up a bed of guitars that could support it. It inspired my writing a lot during that time, specifically a song I wrote while on that tour called “Our Strange Ways.” This record feels hypnotic and deeply meditative. And listening to it as I felt, quite literally, like a prisoner of the white lines on the freeway, was an experience I will never forget. One of my top Joni records of all time.

Long country drives are still my favorite way to pass the time, and Hejira captures why better than any other record I’ve heard. There was a year maybe where I’d point the car in some direction and only play Hejira, on a loop, until I’d memorized every melodic variation and phrase, as if getting a handle on the twists and turns of those infinite songs would give me a better handle on the twists and turns of life itself. I love the interior drama, the humor, the mise en scène, the acceptance of uncertainty and change. The chords, the tunings, obviously. My dad idolized Jaco growing up and makes his own fretless basses, so I hear my dad playing with Joni on the Jaco songs.

Once when I was making lectures for a songwriting class I was undeservingly teaching, I tried writing one about, forgive me, the “multi-perspectival sublime.” I wanted to relate Hejira to the painting “Las Meninas” by Velázquez and how, the longer you look at both, the harder it is to make sense of you-the-viewer’s place in it. Looking at “Las Meninas,” at first the viewer feels that everyone in the painting is looking baldly at them, but as you look closer, you realize the “viewer” is in an impossible position, and likely isn’t in the room at all. The songs on Hejira do this for me. They seem to be about the self, but the perspective shifts rapidly, from a man and a woman sitting on a rock to a blue motel room to a marble bowling ball, from a roadside gas station to the cosmos, a chimney becomes a flag reflected from a bank window into a hotel room — the center is always shifting, to such a degree that the viewer loses their sense of self and surrenders to liminality in a sort of holy way.

I didn’t finish the essay because it’s hard to write about a feeling like that without reducing it to platitudes, and I’m no Peter Schjeldahl. But Hejira really does help me transcend the self, with its trick mirrors and micro-to-macro shifts and its sense of spiritual surrender and leggerezza. It’s my deepest musical attachment, no question.

God, this record. I had a dream once where Joni was sitting on a dock on a lake in Canada singing “Coyote,” with all my family in the water, singing along in the sun. Needless to say, this record and Joni’s voice has been extremely influential to me, even making its way into my dreams!

The freedom in this record, the six-, seven-, eight-minute long songs, her storytelling, taking you on the long and winding road with her. She always reminds me there are no rules. I think my favorite song is “Amelia”: “It was the hexagram of the heavens/It was the strings of my guitar.” She is the master. I am so grateful to have been introduced to Joni so young, her voice as a North Star.

Something I love and admire about Joni is that she never made the same record twice, even though she easily could have, considering how strong her lyrics are on their own. I love the way Joni uses the electric guitar on Hejira. To me, it sounds like rain running down the window of a moving car, which feels so fitting when you think of the record as a kind of travel diary.

I remember the first time I heard “Amelia.” I kept thinking, how does she write a song about someone or something so far removed from my own life, and yet make me see so much of myself in it? Or the way she uses the Cold War as a metaphor in “Blue Motel Room.” That’s what Joni’s lyrics do. They hold a mirror up to whoever is listening without ever seeming to try too hard. Something I often ask myself when I’m writing, especially when listening to a song like “Blue Motel Room,” is how to bring the wider world into the microcosm of everyday life. How do you take something so vast and make it feel so intimate? Joni does that beautifully, and I think it really shines through on Hejira.

Joni Mitchell is one of those songwriters that I go to whenever I have writer’s block — she always provides a well of inspiration. My song “Keep You” is a direct homage to “Coyote” that evoked a scandalous song about love through a free spirit. Lines like “you’ll be brushing out a brood mare’s tail” were scrubbed into imagery like “brushing out the mane of a silver healer.” I love to pull from Joni’s work. She is a huge inspiration to me.

I don’t even know where to begin with Hejira, because it has touched my life in so many profound ways. At first, when I was little and just old enough to hum along to the melodies. Again, when I was a few years older and learning how to play “Coyote” on the guitar. And then a few years later, when I started reading the lyrics of songs I liked and being inspired to start writing my own, which led to my career in songwriting. I remember driving from Maine to L.A. in pursuit of my dream, during which I, of course, listened to Hejira, because I felt as though I was living every lyric in real time. Now as a 34-year-old woman, I continue to return to it as if it’s a friend going through all the same growing pains I’m going through — constantly in search of something, and simultaneously asking if the big dream is worth the loneliness that often comes with it. Even though it’s nearly impossible to choose a favorite song from the record because they are all so intertwined to me, if I had to pick, I’d say “Amelia.” Everything about it. The chord changes. The guitar tones. And of course the perfectly poetic yet heart-wrenchingly clear lyrics that describe two women choosing ambition, exploration, and the unknown. I’m forever grateful to Joni for this album, and my life would be drastically different without it.

Hejira lives in its own world, a sonic-travelogue written on Mitchell’s 1976 journey across America. It’s her most cinematic album too, filled with restless wonder and the characters she’d met along the way. The album was born out of the end of Mitchell’s relationship with drummer John Guerin. They’d lived and toured together. “We had a hard time letting each other go,” says Mitchell today. Her popularity was at a peak after Court and Spark, but a tour of America’s arenas left her missing the intimacy and sound of smaller venues and clubs. She cancelled an upcoming European tour, went skating on Madison, Wisconsin’s icy Lake Mendota (the “bird in flight” series was memorably captured by photographer Joel Bernstein) and headed back to California with the notion that it was time to travel, soak up life, seek new inspiration, and find a course-correction before she became “another scribe writing about the life of a rock singer, a minority experience to be sure.”

Life soon arrived with an invitation. Mitchell’s old friend from Toronto, Australian race-champion Vic Wilson, visited Mitchell with his flight-attendant friend Steven. Wilson was looking to borrow a car for a road-trip to Damariscotta, Maine, where he planned to collect his daughter, Larissa, and return to Australia. Mitchell not only loaned them the Bluebird, her white Mercedes coupe, but enthusiastically joined them with guitar, a suitcase, and sketchpads. (Her car would soon break down and need to be replaced on the road.) Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Marry at Palm Springs Wedding

Parting company with her road-trip buddies in New York city, Mitchell rode back alone. It was America’s Bicentennial summer. With roadmaps (and no driver’s license), she worked her way down the East Coast, through Charleston, South Carolina, the pageantry of small town parades, pinball buddies, flag-draped cafes. Though the disguise rarely escaped close examination, Mitchell often wore a red wig and traveled by the name Charlene Latimer. At night she collected the thoughts of the day and wrote songs filled with longing and delight and raw introspection. “I knew it was a growth step for me,” she reflects today, listening to “Song For Sharon” and other songs from the album. She adds one small disappointment. Nearly back home from her solo return, Mitchell stopped to join Bob Dylan’s Rolling Thunder revue for a show in Ft. Worth. Her artist’s portfolio containing all the Hejira drawings were stolen from her hotel room.

The songs remain. Each one is filled with memory and detail and stunning reflection, but don’t forget to listen to Hejira as a whole. There’s a movie in every full-listen. To further appreciate Hejira, it’s also fun to consider what popular music sounded like in the summer of 1976. It was the peak of disco, radio was filled with the Bee Gees, the thump-thump-thump of post-Saturday Night Fever. Heard in context today, especially with the bass explorations of Jaco Pastorious, Hejira sounds like music from another planet. For any fan who joined the Joni Mitchell journey with Blue, the elixir of Hejira is the adventure you didn’t expect. Mitchell’s own rules for writing the album: “Summon a melody and some chords, write the words …then ask yourself if you’ve done anything like it before. If you have, start over.”

Singer and songwriter Joni Mitchell poses for portrait 1976 in Los Angeles, California.

Photograph by Ginny Winn/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images

#3289. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 rank among the best noise-canceling earbuds on the market, though their usual price tag isn't for the faint of heart. Fortunately, Black Friday has brought them down to a far more approachable, and record-low, price.

Right now, Amazon has the AirPods Pro 3 on sale for $149, knocking a full $100 off retail. If you've been waiting to upgrade to Apple’s best audio and iPhone integration for way less, this is the here's your chance.

Apple’s best wireless earbuds have dropped to their cheapest price yet, taking a full $100 off the standard price tag. Alongside improved audio quality, stronger active noise cancellation, and extra battery life, you’re getting a redesigned, more comfortable build engineered for a secure fit.

Budget wireless earbuds seem like a steal, right up until you lose them. Replacing one misplaced pair after another quickly erases those upfront savings, which is where the AirPods Pro 3 and Apple’s Find My integration come in.

Unlike cheap buds, every AirPod links directly to the Find My network, letting you track down individual earbuds from your iPhone even when they aren't inside the charging case. Better yet, Precision Finding on the AirPods Pro 3 guides you straight to their exact spot rather than leaving you guessing inside a general radius. No tracking system is foolproof, of course, but it puts budget alternatives to shame.

Beyond peace of mind, the AirPods Pro 3 pack serious audio upgrades. Apple has noticeably boosted active noise cancellation, and the latest iOS update adds a sliding scale that lets you dial in full ANC, Transparency mode, or a custom middle ground between the two. You also get up to 8 hours of listening time on a single charge with ANC switched on, stretching to 24 hours total with the charging case.

The everyday extras make them even more versatile. You get Apple Intelligence live translation, built-in heart rate monitoring for workouts, and IP57 dust, sweat, and water resistance. Apple also added new XXS ear tips for anyone who found past AirPods models too large, along with flexible charging via USB-C, MagSafe, or an Apple Watch charger.

If you’ve been eyeing a pair, move fast. Steep discounts on Apple audio gear tend to sell out quickly, and waiting around in hopes of a deeper Black Friday price drop is unlikely to beat this all-time low.

#3287. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Yes, Apple participates in Cyber Monday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy, Amazon, and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3286. Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents …

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

#3283. iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3281. Watch Miranda Lambert Perform Medley of Her Hits at Dallas Cowboys Halftime Show

You can tell that Miranda Lambert is from Texas, but, until today, she’d never performed for her hometown football team — or anyone in the NFL, for that matter. Singing a medley of her classic hits (which she affectionately called “bangers and mash,” i.e., a mashup of her bangers), Lambert made her halftime show debut during the Thanksgiving Day matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium.

Following a pretaped introduction by Reba McEntire, who announced Lambert as the “most awarded artist in the history of the Academy of Country Music,” the Grammy-winning singer took the stage to perform “Snakeskin Boots” (sorry, no Ella Langley cameo), “Kerosene,” “Gunpowder & Lead,” “Mama’s Broken Heart,” and “Little Red Wagon.” Lambert was backed by her band, along with a string section wearing black cowboy hats to mirror that of the entertainer: Lambert, in a black hat, wore a black dress adorned with blue fames. She also received an assist from an army of Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, who delivered their choreographed routine as Lambert sang.

Lambert is a lifelong Cowboys fan who grew up in Lindale, Texas, about 80 miles east of Dallas. She now joins a cast of music’s biggest names as a halftime show veteran, including Beyoncé, Reba McEntire, LeAnn Rimes, Lainey Wilson, and Dolly Parton, who gave a memorable performance while wearing the iconic Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders costume. Coined the “Salvation Army’s 30th Red Kettle Kickoff,” it was McEntire who performed at the inaugural broadcast, which kicks off the annual holiday fundraising drive. Lambert, true to form, announced her appearance from atop a longhorn bull. “It’s my first time ever to do this,” Lambert said during a visit to the Calm Down With Erin and Charissa podcast. “I’ve been doing this 23 years, and it’s my first halftime show ever. Isn’t that crazy? I don’t have a lot of firsts in my career at this point, but I was like okay, here we go.”

It’s been a packed year for Lambert: her album Crisco came out in October, and she just took home a handful of CMA Awards for her work as producer and writer on Ella Langley’s Dandelion and song “Choosin’ Texas.” Next up is the Grammy Awards, where she is nominated seven times and could potentially make history if she wins Producer of the Year.

In line with the company’s design language, these headphones feature transparent elements and bold, geometric detailing that make them stand out from typical matte-black pairs. But the appeal goes beyond the look. These IP52-rated headphones use 40mm drivers, hybrid ANC, and both USB-C and 3.5mm connectivity. They also support high-res audio via LDAC, while Nothing’s companion app gives you basic and advanced EQ controls for adjusting the sound. Battery life is impressive, too, stretching to 35 hours with ANC on and up to 80 hours with it switched off.

But the hardware alone doesn’t define the experience—Nothing’s control scheme is what makes these wireless headphones stand out. Instead of touch panels or clunky buttons, you get a satisfying volume scroll wheel (they call it the Roller), a multi-function Paddle for track navigation, and a customizable button that can switch EQ profiles or noise modes. You also get spatial audio and multipoint Bluetooth support, which work well across Android and iOS.

That said, the earcups aren’t the softest for long sessions, and while they’re padded, the shape might not suit everyone. Performance-wise, the ANC handles low-end noise well (think airplane engines and AC hum) but struggles with sharper, unexpected sounds like clanging dishes or chatter nearby. As for its sound profile, it leans towards the punchier side, especially with a bit of EQ tweaking in the app, but you’ll need to put in some effort if you want the best results, notes this PCMag review.

#3279. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#3277. iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

The iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

#3273. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, for Black Friday, it’s down to $179, which is the lowest price we've seen.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. #3271. Things 3.25 update brings new touch features to the MacBook Pro

Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

Black Friday is a great time to save up on your favorite gadgets, but it's also a fantastic time to pick up a new board or card game. I've been playing board games for as long as I can remember — about 20 years now. My first game was Scrabble, which I still play with my family and partner.

Board games have come a long way, and they're still an excellent way to bond with your family and friends. The holidays are almost upon us, so I highly recommend grabbing either a classic or a brand new one this week. As Tom's Guide's resident board games expert, I've rounded up the best Black Friday deals for you.

My favorite deal is on Catan which is 51% off right now. This is a phenomenal and highly addictive strategy game for up to four players. If you want a more simple game to play with kids and adults alike, get the Magnetic Chess Game for just $8.

If you fancy a card game instead, P for Pizza is my top recommendation, and you can get it for $9 today. Or if you're hosting an adults-only games night, you can't go wrong with Cards Against Humanity which is down to $23 for Black Friday.

Regardless of what you're into, there's a deal for everyone, so allow me to take you through the best Black Friday board and card game deals. And let me know in the comments which game you'll be playing!

By day, I review consumer tech for a living. By night, I'm playing either video games or board/card games. I've loved board and card games since I was a child. My favorites are Scrabble, Catan and Monopoly, and I also thoroughly enjoy silly card games like P for Pizza and Herd Mentality.

When I visited my family a couple of months ago, we spent hours playing this Magnetic Chess Game. One player makes a shape with the included string and other players must place their magnetic pieces without touching the others. It's a great game for adults and kids alike.

This is one for whodunnit and murder mystery fans. Clue is discounted for Black Friday, and is a great game to play with friends and family over the holidays. In this murder mystery board game, you and up to six other players act as detectives to solve a murder. You must figure out who committed the crime, the weapon they used, and which room the crime took place in. Other players will try to ruin your strategy by using cards in their hands, and the first person to make an accurate accusation wins.

Do you like board games that are equal parts visually aesthetic and fun? Try Azul! It's a tactile game about tile laying. The mosaic tiles are inspired by Portuguese azulejos. It's easy to learn and deceptively deep in strategy, and works great at just about any player count. If you're not feeling the tile laying, there's a chocolate variant and three sequels that offer different rules and shaped pieces.

I'm sure you've played Monopoly hundreds of times (just me? Okay...), but if you haven't, what are you waiting for? Monopoly's an all-time classic. You and up to five other players buy, sell and scheme your way to becoming the richest person alive. You can build houses and hotels and trade these if a player offers you a better deal. Warning: may cause (friendly) arguments!

Few board games come close to being as great as this one. Catan is a highly addictive strategy game for three to four players which turns you into hard-nosed settlers, competing to conquer an island. You must collect resource cards to build roads, village and cities, but collecting them heavily relies on dice rolls and trading with other players. Oh, and there's a resource-stealing robber too to spice things up, so watch out!

When we're having a cozy date night, P for Pizza is a game my partner and I always play. In this fast-paced card game, you have to shout out a word that links the letter on one card to the category on another (on a pile in the middle of the table). For example, a food that starts with G, an actress whose name begins with K, a stringed instrument that starts with S, and so on. You need to be quick to add a slice to your pile, and the first one to form a 'pizza slice' wins.

Need a party game for the holidays? Try Herd Mentality. It's easy to pick up and play as all you need to do is flip a card and read out a random question like, "Who is the most popular female artist of all time?" You and the other players then write down the answer you think will be the most common among the group. If you're in the majority, you win points; if not, you'll be left with the dreaded pink cow of doom. And as someone who adores cows, you don't want to get stuck with this one...

If you want a fast-paced board/card game where you deduce your fellow players' behavior, The Chameleon is for you. In this game, everyone know a secret word except one hidden imposter. Each player gives a single related clue to prove they belong without revealing too much. The group then votes to unmask the traitor... or Chameleon, if you will. Each round can last as long as the group likes.

The first time I played You Can't Say UMM was at a board games café with my friends. We laughed so much that our jaws hurt and we had tears running down our faces. In this card game, you have to describe an object to your teammate without saying "Umm" or "Err." The opposing team can catch you out and penalize you. Opponents can also add "rules" to your turn, such as, "Swap seats with a teammate after every correct guess." It's harder than it sounds, and it's a barrel of laughs.

Cards Against Humanity is the perfect card game for adults — and to determine who among your friend group has the darkest humor. One player reads a fill-in-the-blank prompt from a black card, and everyone else submits their funniest, most offensive, or absurd white answer card. The reader picks the winner, awarding a point. It can get really horrible really fast — but it's oh so fun.

My partner and I play Ransom Notes with our friends fairly often. In this game, you and the other players race against a timer to answer outrageous prompts using only a limited handful of random word magnets. Everyone reads their grammatically chaotic sentences aloud while a rotating judge picks the funniest response to award a point. The first to five points (or the number of your choosing) wins!

#3269. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3265. CarPlay Ultra coming to these cars, according to Apple

Last year, Apple officially announced CarPlay Ultra, the next-generation version of CarPlay that it first teased way back at WWDC 2022.

CarPlay Ultra first launched for Aston Martin owners in the United States and Canada. What about other automakers? Here’s what we know.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Updated November 24, 2026: Latest on Hyundai, more.

In December 2023, Apple said that Porsche and Aston Martin would be the first automakers to support next-generation CarPlay starting in 2024. That deadline came and went, and Apple confirmed in January that next-gen CarPlay had been delayed but was still in development.

Apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The company also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

When Apple announced the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three new partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

However, several brands have also dropped their plans to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that said, here is the full list of automakers who plan to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of November 2026.

What do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai announced the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major new Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

In a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the company is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:

“We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

The question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.
