#3194. This Low-Profile Roborock Vacuum and Mop Is $500 Off During Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3191. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3190. Get a Head Start on the New Year With the Best Smartwatches and Fitness Trackers on Sale for Black Friday

Black Friday sales are in full swing, and I've been keeping an eye on all the best fitness trackers and smartwatch deals so that you can snag the best possible price from now until the end of Cyber Monday (Nov. 30). Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is a worthy competitor to the Oura Ring 5, with an included high-capacity charging case and no subscription. You can read Beth's comparison of the two here: most people would probably prefer the Oura, but the pros and cons are nuanced and you, dear reader, may be exactly the person the Ultrahuman is best for. The silver color is only $299 in this Black Friday deal, with other colors going for $379. The ring normally retails for $479, so that's $100 to $180 off, depending on color. That price includes a charging case and all the basic functionality of the ring; some extras require a subscription.

This is a rare deal from Pebble! An email from the company states "We don’t do sales. Black Friday is the one exception each year." The Pebble Time 2 is on sale for $200, down from $225 regular price. This is the brand's rectangular watch, with a heart rate sensor, and an always-on MIP (e-paper) screen. The Pebble 2 Duo (a "do-over" version of the Pebble of yore) is also on sale, for $124, down from $149.

The Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. These are the lowest prices ever for these rings, which usually go for $399 and $499, respectively. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I've tried, although it's worth noting it requires a $5.99/month subscription fee.

For an even cheaper deal, the older Oura Ring 4 is $249—a full $100 off its list price of $349. If you opt for "stealth" (matte black), the price is $279; for gold, it's $286.61, down from $399. While this model has since been replaced by the Oura Ring 5, it's still an accurate and comfortable smart ring—especially if tracking your sleep is your priority.

Whoop may be one of the most expensive smart bands out there, thanks to its subscription-only model. But that price is particularly low right now, since the Peak membership that normally goes for $239 is now $199. Peak is the middle tier, and it's the one Beth recommends. While you can get Whoop One for $189 in this sale, the $10 you save isn't really worth it given the features you'd be missing. We also wouldn't normally recommend Whoop Life, since its ECG readings and blood pressure estimates aren't really worth the extra cost. That said, if you do want it, the Life tier is $299 right now instead of $359.

The new Luna band is on sale for $119.20, down from a normal price of $149. The Luna band is made by Indian smartwatch company Noise, the same company behind the Luna Ring that Beth reviewed last year. The ring is no longer available in the U.S., but the band is. It's a Whoop-style screenless fitness tracker, potentially a worthy competitor to the Fitbit Air and other smart bands.

This is the brand-new Apple Watch model, and it's actually worth the upgrade. One of the biggest reasons is that the Series 12's new processor (called, confusingly, the S11 chip) supports some features older Apple Watches can't, and a good rule of thumb is that whenever there's a break in software compatibility, it makes sense to get the newer model. Right now, we're seeing it for as low as $299, down from the list price of $399. (And if you're stuck deciding between an Apple Watch and a Fitbit, Beth breaks it all down in her comparison of the two watches.)

The Google Pixel Watch 5 has been marked down by $100, starting at $299.99 for the version that normally retails for $399.99. Each model is $100 off its regular price, including the LTE and Wifi-only models of both sizes.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is Nothing's latest smartwatch, and it incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT; you can currently pick it up at a major discount. Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $55. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been.

If you're looking specifically for a sporty, outdoors watch, Garmin sets the standard. (You could definitely call Meredith something of a Garmin enthusiast.) Here are the best Black Friday deals on Garmin watches that we've seen so far:

The 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 is 249.99 (down from $449.99). The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class—a must for those going off-grid.

The Garmin Fēnix 8 in titanium with a gray band is $749.99 (down from $999.99). While this is last year's model, it's a perfectly solid option if you don't specifically need the titanium case or the latest mapping engine in the latest Fenix 9 Pro.

The Garmin Forerunner 265 is $299.99 (down from $449.99). Although it isn't the latest and greatest anymore, this is still a fan favorite among Garmin users. It's a step above entry-level options, with dual-band GPS, power meter compatibility, and advanced analytics (like training status).

Meredith's beloved Forerunner 970, the top-of-the-line Garmin for serious runners, is $649.99 right now, down from an original price of $749.99.

Yes, Garmin is one of the best brands when it comes to rugged sports watches and fitness trackers. The Forerunner line, especially, is a go-to pick for accurate and reliable GPS tracking for runners.

My pick would be the Garmin Forerunner 265 for $299.99. It's a slightly older model, but still works well and is packed with features for runners.

There are! Check out the Apple Watch deals above. If you can't decide, my pick would be the brand-new Series 12 at $299. This one has step counting and will soon be getting the slightly creepy Siri Recaps (which you can disable if you'd rather not deal with them).

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. #3186. These Beats Solo 4 Headphones Are 50% Off at Walmart for Black Friday

Beats has a long history of making on-ear headphones that stand with the plushest and best-sounding cans on the market. As Black Friday deals are here, it's a great time to upgrade: Walmart has discounted the Beats Solo 4 by more than 50% to $99.95 (originally $199.95); the sale applies to the black, pink, and slate blue variants.

These headphones don’t have ANC, just passive isolation, but they still deliver solid sound, comfort, and strong battery life. They use physical controls and support one-touch pairing with most Apple devices, as well as hands-free Siri. The Solo 4 headphones are compatible with Bluetooth 5.3 and work with the AAC and SBC codecs. They also support wired audio via 3.5mm or USB-C.

The headphones last around 50 hours per charge (about 10 hours longer than their predecessor), and 10 minutes of charging gives you around five hours of playback, with a full recharge taking approximately two hours. In its review, PCMag describes the sound as “sculpted with accentuated bass and highs."

Although they lack ANC and adjustable EQ, these headphones still have plenty of extra features for Apple users, and those shortcomings are much easier to forgive at 50% off. For $99, the Beats Solo 4 headphones are a compact and well-equipped option for casual listening, with long battery life and that classic Beats aesthetic.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are 45% off right now, down to $199 for Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Colors include in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3182. Major MacBook Air ‘overhaul’ could launch next year, per Gurman

Apple has a new MacBook Air with M6 chip coming early next year, but per Mark Gurman on his latest podcast episode, a “big MacBook Air overhaul” could launch as early as 2027 too. Here’s what he said.

Today on the latest episode of Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the well-sourced reporter answered a listener question that involves the future of the MacBook Air.

When asked about the next-generation MacBook Air, here’s what Gurman said:

The next MacBook Air project, J913 and J915, the 13-inch version and the 15-inch version, that is coming in spring 2027 alongside the MacBook Neo 2. And this is going to be another “chip and ship,” so a chip refresh.

And we are getting to the end of the road here for the current MacBook Air design. The current MacBook Air design was introduced in ’22, was refreshed in ’23 with the 15-inch model. We’re now in 2027. MacBook Air is Apple’s most popular computer, and they need to keep it very fresh. And so my anticipation is 2027-2028 is when we’re going to get the big MacBook Air overhaul. And I think OLED will be part of that conversation.

There are several noteworthy takeaways here:

It would be unusual for Apple to launch two distinct MacBook Air models in the same calendar year. However, if that does happen, it would follow the exact same playbook Apple used with the MacBook Pro this year.

Of course it's getting an 'overhaul' (whatever that means for a MacBook that will largely look and work the exact same) because it needs to replace the MacBook Pros pricing structure. Now that the Neo exists, the Air line needs to be exponentially more expensive because that's how Apple operates these days. Give you the absolute bare bones minimum at a huge premium and then absolutely soak anyone who needs anything of value.

This March, a new MacBook Pro launched with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips but the same design that’s been around since 2021. Then in October, Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display and a new industrial design.

It sounds like a very similar rollout could happen for the MacBook Air in 2027.

You can watch Mark Gurman’s latest podcast episode below.

Are you interested in a redesigned MacBook Air with OLED? Let us know in the comments.

#3181. Firefox now spends 27% of its effort on security fixes, up from 10%

Ajit Varma says AI models are finding more complex bugs, but his team still has time to keep up.

The Firefox browser app shown on a smartphone in front of the Firefox logo.

Mozilla’s Firefox team now spends 27% of its effort fixing security flaws, up from about 10% a year ago, Firefox head Ajit Varma told Business Insider. OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla free access to models that are finding more complex bugs.

Mozilla’s Firefox team now spends 27% of its effort fixing security flaws, up from about 10% a year ago, Firefox head Ajit Varma told Business Insider. The rise comes as AI models find more bugs in the browser.

Varma said OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla, a nonprofit, “a lot of tokens for free”. Their models, he said, “are finding more and more complicated vulnerabilities within our browser.”

In April, Mozilla patched 271 Firefox bugs found by Anthropic’s Mythos. OpenAI’s new GPT-6 Cyber model has since turned up 81 more. Rival browsers face the same surge: Chrome patched a record 429 bugs in June.

Varma still thinks the pace of AI gives his team “enough time” to fix problems before the next leap. He is also using AI to make Firefox faster and stop memory leaks.

“There’s a lot of routine activities that we don’t necessarily need humans to do and that AI does really well because it’s relentless; it doesn’t get tired,” he said.

Others are less relaxed. Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella warned last week that AI-found bugs mean more outages, as companies rush out fixes faster than they can test them.

This joins the existing ability to adjust snow amount, flake size, fall speed, and wind direction.

Head to the Festivitas website to get started and bring some holiday cheer to your Apple devices.

#3177. Microsoft says China’s Salt Typhoon and North Korean hackers now use ARTEX

Microsoft says the tool, now in Salt Typhoon’s hands, can reach privileged access within minutes. Its report explains how ARTEX works, who sells it, and the bursts that give it away.

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York

State-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft says. Microsoft Threat Intelligence named the groups in a report published on Wednesday.

The list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean. Two more clusters, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358, are also on it. Microsoft says state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers use ARTEX to speed up network scans, credential attacks, and attacks on web apps.

“Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes,” Microsoft wrote.

The report landed hours after US media tied ARTEX to the hack of three US spy agencies, as Jonathan Greig reported for The Record.

US agencies believe Salt Typhoon breached at least nine telecoms groups in 2024, The Record noted. That hack allegedly reached phones used by Donald Trump and JD Vance. A US House report later said Chinese carriers were still inside American phone networks.

Crystal Typhoon is newer. It was first seen in late 2023 and goes after government networks and critical infrastructure through edge devices and firewalls, TechRadar reported.

Microsoft had already linked Storm-0940 to the ConnectWise supply chain attack. The new report adds numbers from its campaigns. In one, Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 a minute. In several intrusions, the attackers had privileged access less than three hours after they first went after a target.

In another case, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

A GitHub user called Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese interface in July. The developer took it down in October, but other developers kept publishing their own versions. This month, the Chinese security firm ThreatBook claimed ownership and started selling access to “ARTEX Pro”.

The attacker sets the targets. One AI model breaks the job into goals. A planner agent then hands short tasks to worker agents with a real shell and hacking tools. A reporter agent writes up what worked. ARTEX can run on almost any large language model, including ones stripped of their guardrails. That means no single AI provider’s safety controls can stop it, Microsoft says.

The FBI warned about ARTEX earlier this month.

“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

Attackers can change the tool’s IP addresses and user agent strings, so blocking those alone will not work. The steadiest sign is behaviour: many varied requests in a short burst, and quick moves to the next step. ARTEX does nothing to hide that activity by default.

Microsoft also suggests honeypots, tarpits, and fake wins. A fake win shows the agent false proof that its job is done, so it stops. It recommends rate limits, phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in, and replacing any secret that leaks into code. The report also points customers to Microsoft’s own products, including Defender XDR and its Perception security agents.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday have become two of the biggest shopping events on the Australian retail calendar, making them an ideal time to tackle those larger purchases you've been putting off. Whether you're upgrading your TV, replacing an ageing mattress or investing in a new appliance, many retailers reserve some of their strongest offers of the year for this end-of-year sales period.

While it's impossible to know every deal ahead of time, there are a few trends that tend to repeat each year. Amazon's usually among the top retailers offering with major discounts, particularly across its own range of devices, including Kindle ereaders, smart speakers home security products.

JB Hi-Fi and The Good Guys are also major players across popular tech categories, though buying direct from brands like Dell, Dyson and Samsung can often be the best option in terms of savings. If you've been eyeing a new laptop, desktop PC or other big-ticket electronics purchase, holding off until the sales begin could be a smart move. With competition between retailers at its peak, Black Friday is often when some of the year's most attractive tech deals appear.

Black Friday 2025 falls on Friday, November 27, 2026, with sales extending through Cyber Monday, ending at 11:59 pm (AEST) on Monday, November 30, 2026.

With that in mind, you can anticipate deals starting well ahead of the official launch date. Retailers like Amazon, The Good Guys, Dell and Myer are known for rolling out early discounts, so be sure to watch for great offers in the weeks leading up to the big day.

In Australia, plenty of retailers will be vying to offer the best Black Friday deals and discounts. Which retailer has the best offers really depends on what you're looking to buy. For example, Amazon, The Good Guys, JB Hi-Fi, and Harvey Norman typically provide the biggest savings on 4K TVs, smartphones, and appliances.

If you're in the market for a new PC or laptop, it's a good idea to buy directly from brands like Dell and HP. Also, keep an eye on eBay Australia, which usually has discounts on almost everything, with even bigger savings available for eBay Plus members.

Originating in the United States, the term "Black Friday" in relation to shopping dates back to 1961. It was first used in Philadelphia to describe the heavy pedestrian and vehicle traffic that followed the Thanksgiving holiday.

The term gained popularity and spread nationwide by 1975. Over time, Black Friday took on a new meaning for retailers, signifying the point in the year when businesses went "in the black," finally turning a profit. This allowed them to offer major discounts on leftover stock, resulting in massive deals leading up to the holiday season.

Although the timing differs from one country to another, the Black Friday sales event has become a global phenomenon, which is why Australia now participates.

#3174. Rockstar staff vote 75% against union recognition a week after GTA VI

The Rockstar union vote drew a 93.2% turnout among UK staff. The union says it will keep organising, while a tribunal over the firing of more than 30 members has yet to rule.

Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork featuring Jason and Lucia.

Rockstar Games staff in the UK have voted against recognising a union, a week after the studio launched Grand Theft Auto VI. Three in four votes went against a recognition deal with the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union. The Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) announced the result on Thursday.

About 1,600 staff below director level could vote. Of those, 1,544 took part, a turnout of 93.2%, Chris Kerr reported for Vertical Slice, which broke the result. The ballot ran from 12 to 26 November.

The split was 75.3% against and 24.7% in favour across the Edinburgh, Leeds, Lincoln, Dundee, and London offices, GamesIndustry.biz reported. IGN put the count at 1,163 votes against and 381 for.

A yes vote would have made the branch the largest recognised union in the UK games industry. It would have set up formal talks on pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions. Staff would also have had a say on HR policies and on how Rockstar uses generative AI, Vertical Slice reported.

The union already exists, and staff can still join it. The result means management does not have to hold regular meetings with its representatives. Under UK law, the union cannot apply for recognition again for three years, according to GamesIndustry.biz.

“Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues,” the IWGB said in a statement.

The union said the result “isn’t a sign to retreat”. It will keep pushing for pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against AI and layoffs.

“This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong,” Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar’s head of publishing, said in a statement.

The vote follows a long dispute. In October 2025, Rockstar fired more than 30 staff, all IWGB members. The studio says they leaked confidential information in a Discord channel. The union says those talks were protected union activity and accuses Rockstar of union busting.

The fired workers took the case to an employment tribunal in Glasgow, which heard closing arguments on 19 November. Their lawyers argued the sackings came soon after an informant said union membership was nearing 10% of staff. That is roughly the level needed to apply for recognition. Rockstar’s counsel told the tribunal the workers were “caught red-handed”, Wccftech reported. Judge Lucy Wiseman has not yet ruled.

The ballot overlapped with the biggest launch in Rockstar’s history. GTA VI made $3.79 billion in a record first day, after it tied Metacritic’s record with a 99. Take-Two has said the game was built without generative AI.

#3172. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3170. Signal’s Moxie Marlinspike says AI safety is building mass surveillance

Marlinspike told Tyler Cowen that AI surveillance should target the models, not the people using them. He also pitched Confer, his private chatbot, and admitted he can’t say if AI will break encryption.

Moxie Marlinspike, who built Signal, says the way AI companies police misuse is turning into the biggest mass surveillance system ever built. He wants the watching pointed at the AI models instead of the people using them, he told Tyler Cowen on Conversations with Tyler. The episode was recorded live at the Progress Conference on 10 October and published on Wednesday.

“You’re building a machinery of mass surveillance that is larger and more efficient than any other mass surveillance machinery in history,” Marlinspike said.

He described today’s approach as scoring everything users do for “badness” and sending the worst to human reviewers. TNW reported in September that contractors read real ChatGPT conversations.

His alternative is to monitor whether the models themselves show bad tendencies. Labs would train narrow models that each spot one kind of behaviour, then use them to check the general models. Cowen asked whether using AI to watch AI really counts, pointing to the Hugging Face breach. Marlinspike said it does.

Chatbots invite confession because they feel private, Marlinspike said. In practice, chats end up in a data lake used for training and analysis.

“You feel like you’re having this conversation with this agent or assistant that gets to know you as your friend… but actually, it’s a huge group chat with many, many more people,” he said.

He runs Confer, a private AI chat service at confer.to. Only the user can read their chats, he said, and he cannot. Claude and ChatGPT “are not operating private services,” he added, though he said the big labs could build one.

Asked whether the recent flood of AI maths results could break cryptography, Marlinspike answered: “I don’t know.”

“If there is some result that just all of public-key cryptography doesn’t work anymore, then the whole internet is in trouble,” he said.

In that worst case, nobody could trust software updates, websites or online banking. He also described milder outcomes, where some algorithms would only need larger keys. Moving to post-quantum encryption took about five years, he said, and a second switch would likely be faster.

On hacking, he expects a painful period before AI gets as good at patching flaws as at finding them. He put the wait at about a year. Cowen doubted that small cities could patch their systems that fast.

Marlinspike said Signal knows almost nothing about its users. It cannot see their contacts, group names, profile names, searches, or stickers. WhatsApp uses the Signal protocol to encrypt messages, but much of that other data is not protected, he said. Signal recently moved to block AI agents from reading chats.

Cowen also asked what the 2025 Pentagon group chat on Signal had done for the app.

“It made it all worth it for me,” Marlinspike said.

#3168. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release by mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

Expect to see iOS 27.3 launch as early as the week of December 7, or on Monday, December 14 at the latest.

#3166. Firms set up memory chip ‘war rooms’ as some prices jump 10x, WSJ reports

The memory chip shortage has staff trawling eBay and brokers for a handful of chips. Even Elon Musk got no special deal from Samsung’s chairman, according to a second-hand account.

Electronics makers have set up procurement “war rooms” to hunt for memory chips. Prices for some chips have risen tenfold in a year, Jiyoung Sohn and Sooyoung Rhee reported for The Wall Street Journal. Staff scour eBay, call hundreds of brokers and buy batches as small as five to 12 units, the newspaper found.

Smaller firms are hit hardest. Large buyers can lock in supply through long-term deals with the chipmakers. Others rely on brokers and the grey market. Some sellers there mix used chips into orders of new ones, the Journal reported.

“Suddenly, I’ll hear a string of bad language and ask what’s going on,” Blackmagic Design chief executive Grant Petty told the Journal.

Taiwanese memory module maker Apacer has taken out loans so it has cash ready whenever supply appears, according to the report.

“If chips show up, we take it. This is crazy, but there is no other way,” Apacer president Gibson Chen told the Journal.

Thieves took about $100,000 of flash memory from one company’s warehouse in Indonesia, the paper reported. The firm suspects a former employee.

The Journal also carried a second-hand account of a meeting between Elon Musk and Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong. Capital Group’s Carl Kawaja said Musk told him about it in June. Musk asked for a long-term memory deal, and Lee replied that everyone offers that.

“We get that offer from everyone. What else can you do for us?” Lee asked, according to Kawaja’s account.

Musk then offered to guarantee financing for a new Samsung chip plant, Kawaja said, and got the same answer. TNW has not independently verified the account. Sam Altman has also courted the company, meeting Samsung’s presidents in October.

The shortage comes as Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron move production to the high-bandwidth memory used in AI chips. SK Hynix has said tight supply could last until 2030.

Consumers are already paying. In India, around 48 Samsung and Xiaomi phone models went up by ₹1,000 to ₹4,000 in mid-November, Inc42 reported. Samsung’s Galaxy A07 5G now costs ₹22,999, up from ₹20,999.

AI start-ups are feeling it in the cloud. GPU rental prices in India have risen 30% to 35% since February, Subhashish Banerjee, co-founder of Bharat1 AI, told Inc42. Providers now want three to six month commitments from start-ups that once booked a few hours at a time.

Some are cutting their needs instead. SquadStack, which runs voice AI agents, built smaller models trained on its own call data. Fewer tokens per call cut its costs even as hardware got pricier, chief executive Apurv Agrawal told Inc42. Memory costs have also hit Xiaomi’s quarterly profit and Apple’s margins.

#3165. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3164. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3163. Binance fully reopens withdrawals nearly a month after its $6.3B hack

Binance withdrawals are open again across almost every network. The exchange says it covered the stolen assets with $6.34 billion of its own money, while the hackers keep moving funds.

Richard Teng, then Binance’s head of regional markets, at Binance Blockchain Week 2023 in Istanbul.

Binance has lifted the last of the withdrawal limits it put in place after its record $6.3 billion hack in October. The exchange said on Thursday that its withdrawal recovery work is complete.

“Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the October security incident has been fully lifted,” Binance said.

A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance or planned upgrades. Binance said those pauses cover a very small share of normal traffic and are separate from the recovery.

Binance halted withdrawals after the breach on 29 October and began restoring them on 1 November, starting with Bitcoin. Deposits stayed open throughout, crypto.news reported.

The first day brought a rush. Customers took out $4.65 billion and put in $1.01 billion in the first nine and a half hours on 1 November, the exchange said. That left a net outflow of $3.64 billion. Binance reopened 87 more networks in the week to 14 November.

The exchange has said it covered the stolen assets with more than $6.34 billion of its own money. It drew on its corporate treasury, part of its user protection fund and part of its futures insurance fund. It has pledged to rebuild the user fund to about $1 billion, and published a reserve snapshot covering 198 tokens.

Wallets linked to the hack moved another $35.52 million in Ether on Thursday, according to blockchain tracker Onchain Lens. It put the hackers’ remaining unfrozen holdings at about $1.9 billion.

US authorities and private companies have frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen crypto. The Justice Department also won court approval to seize more than $1.2 billion of it, The Block reported on 12 November.

The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the theft. Binance said a fake job interview gave the attackers their way in. Days after the hack, the exchange insisted it was in ‘very strong’ health.

#3162. Report: Apple gains ground as Latin American smartphone shipments plunge 24% in Q3

According to a new Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research says the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”

Per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:

Apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”
